Within these frameworks, the pressure tensor is expressed as a deviation from the Navier-Stokes behavior, parameterized by specific coefficients. These coefficients can be determined either through rigorous kinetic theory or, more efficiently, via non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD), which offers a pathway to model liquid and gas phases where kinetic approaches fail. In this study, we demonstrate that machine learning (ML) serves as a powerful alternative to NEMD for simulating flow processes. We introduce a model where the pressure tensor is represented as a neural network dependent on the velocity gradient and material properties. We validate this approach on a simple monatomic system using both a model based on the Enskog kinetic theory and one trained on molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of a Lennard-Jones fluid. When these newly developed coefficients are applied to Enkogs or Enkogs-Fourier models, the resulting simulations for shear flow and shock waves align closely with established benchmark results.

In this paper, the dynamics of an isolated two-dimensional palm tree vortex are analyzed under conditions of strong rotation-stratification coupling, specifically the Taylor-Proudman regime where the Coriolis and buoyancy frequencies are nearly equal ($f \approx N$). The analysis reveals that the flow organizes into two parallel bands aligned along the primary axis of rotation, separated by a transverse barrier that prevents fluid exchange. The separation between these bands is modulated by the Rossby number ($\epsilon$), which quantifies the relative importance of Coriolis and pressure gradient forces.

While frequently observed in confined geometries, such abrupt changes can also arise in bulk materials, a phenomenon known as a Luders jump. In these bulk cases, distinct domains rich in shear bands and elastic bands occupy adjacent regions defined by a narrow transition zone. This article examines the origins of both the shear band-Luders jump connection and the overall bulk phenomenon, utilizing a two-mode constitutive framework. This model incorporates a primary mode responsible for instantaneous viscoelasticity and a secondary mode governing gradual structural evolution, featuring a mechanism akin to a phase transition that drives the formation of banding. It is demonstrated that standard models, which treat the second mode as a simple time delay, fail to generate the characteristic discontinuities. Conversely, introducing thermodynamic equilibrium between modes yields a predictive link between bulk and localized phenomena, utilizing this formalism to match experimental data from polymers exhibiting shear banding.

While prior studies have examined these effects in face-to-face environments, the effects of remote work remain under-researched. To address this gap, this paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for innovation driven by virtual work. It posits that digital-mediated remote work alters communication behaviors, which subsequently reshapes innovation outcomes. Validated through empirical analysis of data from 440 European executives across 440 firms using structural equation modeling, these findings offer fresh insights into how remote work influences innovation. Furthermore, the study identifies critical yet previously unexplored mechanisms, specifically the diminished frequency of weak-tie interactions and the erosion of social trust within virtual work settings.

of an extensive continental breakup that involved both the Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico, yet current understanding relies on fragmented data due to an absence of integrated seismic surveys across this region. To address this, we utilized high-resolution multichannel seismic (MCS) records collected during a 2019 Geological Society of America (GSA) field trip along a transect stretching from western Brazil to western Africa across nearly the full breadth of the South Atlantic Ocean basin. These datasets were integrated with existing seismic, bathymetric, and gravity measurements to generate the most comprehensive geophysical atlas of the South Atlantic rift system to date. Our findings reveal that the continental breakup occurred along divergent pathways: western Africa experienced lateral spreading relative to the central and eastern sectors of the nascent ocean, whereas western Brazil remained stationary while eastern parts of the South American plate moved away from North and South America. The continental crust along the entire rifting track displays a broad spectrum of architectures, ranging from incomplete initial stages through transitional phases to fully formed continental margins, with crustal anomalies like intrusions and rift valleys clearly visible throughout. Furthermore, we identified a previously undocumented ultra-wide ultra-shallow (USUL) axial valley on the ultra-central (CU) mid-ocean ridge, characterized by distinct structural features including parallel arms, roof structures, and multiple interconnected sub-valleys.

$-dependent functions, termed Generalized Parton Holographic Functions (GHFs), which are conjectured to represent a novel $k_\perp$-dependent factor in high-energy physics processes. These functions are defined as integrals over all kinematically allowed $k_\perp$ values, utilizing a parton holographic distribution that depends on both $k_\perp$ and the specific process under study. Our proposal introduces a fresh perspective on factorization in high-energy collisions by extending the parton holographic distribution to include non-perturbative $k_\perp$ components. This approach incorporates both perturbative and non-perturbative $k_\perp$ dependencies within a unified framework, thereby generalizing the traditional "perturbative $k_\perp$ tail." Specifically, we demonstrate that perturbative contributions follow a power law with a process-dependent exponent, whereas the non-perturbative side exhibits an exponential behavior characterized by a universal exponent of approximately 2 GeV. The parton holographic distribution serves as the primary input for these integrals and is shown to possess universal properties. Furthermore, we argue that GHFs function as new parton distributions applicable to various processes, potentially possessing even more universality than conventional parton distribution functions.

These surface states are defined by their linear dispersion relations and protected by topology against backscattering caused by non-magnetic impurities. This study examines the magnetoresistance of thin films comprising bismuth antimonide ($\text{BiSb}$ alloy) and investigates the magnetic field's impact on the magnetoresistance of these topological insulators. The results indicate that at elevated magnetic field strengths, $\text{BiSb}$ alloys exhibit a positive and substantial magnetoresistance, which increases as temperature drops. Furthermore, at room temperature and low-field conditions, a negative magnetoresistance is evident, attributed to the magnetization of paramagnetic impurities within the bulk. The negative magnetoresistance effect diminishes with falling temperatures and is completely eliminated at 77 K. Conversely, the positive high-field magnetoresistance is ascribed to the cyclotron motion of carriers in the bulk, potentially aided by weak interferences from the surface states. Ultimately, the study concludes that for the specific alloy composition analyzed, the contributions from both surface states and bulk carriers are negligible, resulting in negligible quantum oscillations.

the mechanisms behind sudden regime changes are critical concerns in ecology, economics, and social sciences. This study introduces a novel statistical model designed to discover sudden shifts in the dynamic behavior of time series data within these domains. By integrating a regime-switching framework with ecological or physical frictions—such as ecological carrying capacities or market impact costs—we link these structural breaks to specific alterations in system nonlinearity. This study introduces *crowd morphometrics*, a computational framework designed to quantify and analyze these dimensions. We define a set of novel metrics to evaluate the impact of crowd members' body sizes on global and localized movement patterns. Key applications of crowd morphometrics include identifying body-size-dependent thresholds for phase transitions during evacuation, analyzing how physical dimensions influence spatial organization within crowds, and investigating how body size affects movement in response to external forces such as wind pressure.

To formalize body size variation, we introduce the *crowd size distribution* and *crowdedness distribution*. The former quantifies how frequent different size ranges are within a population, while the latter assesses how densely individuals of a specific size are clustered. We utilize these distributions to test various hypotheses linking body size to crowd organization and to forecast critical thresholds of collective motion. We further propose two distinct order parameters that characterize the emergent structures formed by varying size distributions. We demonstrate that traditional order parameters, which typically mark transitions from ordered to disordered crowd states, shift when population size distributions vary, and we develop a generalized parameter to account for these variations.

We validate our computational methods and newly defined metrics through two distinct models: (i) the *multi-force model*, which simulates how wind pressure drives individuals toward an exit, and (ii) the *multi-force-collision model*, which adds repulsive interactions to represent physical collisions between agents.

the **Maximum Weight Independent Set (MWIS)** problem seeks an independent set \(S \subseteq V\) that maximizes \(\sum_{v \in S} w_v\), where \(w_v\) is the weight assigned to vertex \(v\). This problem is known to be NP-hard, implying the absence of a polynomial-time algorithm for it unless P equals NP. Despite this, exact algorithms exist, including branch-and-bound methods, dynamic programming approaches, and integer linear programming formulations. Additionally, several heuristic and approximation algorithms have been developed to generate near-optimal solutions in practical terms.

We demonstrate the application of **machine learning (ML)** to approximate the MWIS solution more effectively. We begin by outlining the learning framework, detailing the selection of the optimal model, and then introduce an iterative refinement strategy that boosts solution quality. This proposed method achieves a solution virtually identical to the true optimum in just a fraction of the computational time required by standard exact algorithms.

beyond-system mobile networks (BSMN) increasingly rely on massive antenna arrays to maximize spectral efficiency. However, the extensive radio frequency (RF) components required for fully distributed RF architectures create prohibitive costs and power consumption issues. To address this, recent research favors radio RF architectures, which consolidate all user equipment (RF) down to the RF layer, significantly reducing both cost and energy use while maintaining high spectral efficiency through distributed base station designs. Despite these benefits, current RF models suffer from oversimplified assumptions regarding channel estimation and feedback, leading to suboptimal resource allocation strategies. In response, we present a comprehensive framework for downlink multi-user MIMO operations under RF architectures, integrating advanced joint transmission methods, codebook selection, and precoding techniques tailored specifically to realistic channel state information constraints. Through extensive numerical simulations, we demonstrate that these proposed joint approaches substantially outperform existing state-of-the-art RF codebook and allocation methods in terms of ergodic sum rate, offering a clear path toward more efficient future mobile systems.

Nevertheless, the specific mechanisms by which these collisions trigger intense starburst activity and central supermassive black hole accretion remain subjects of significant study. This research utilizes high-resolution, three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations to examine accretion into central active galactic nuclei (AGN) and starbursts in colliding star-forming galaxies. We conducted merger simulations across various mass ratios, initial conditions, and central black holes, utilizing a two-fluid model to evaluate outflow rates, accretion bursts, and the potential for successful quenching of central AGN by starbursts. Our simulations reveal that both outflows and burst-like accretion events occur in all merger scenarios, though their timing and magnitude differ substantially. Specifically, feedback from starbursts can temporarily suppress AGN accretion by roughly an order of magnitude immediately following a burst, creating a characteristic "limit cycle" of repeated, intense accretion episodes. While dense gas flows generated during mergers can naturally quench a central AGN, the result is often a preceding burst of star formation that reignites the AGN activity. Consequently, our models indicate that colliding galaxies produce both sudden accretion bursts and outflows, potentially explaining certain classes of powerful, recent AGN outflow detections.

has historically focused on continuous models, understanding the impact of rounding on continuous mechanisms is essential, as most real-world data is naturally rounded. This paper investigates how rounding influences the revenue of mechanism design, specifically examining first-price auctions. We demonstrate that for first-price auctions, rounding data does not significantly diminish revenue; for any $\epsilon$-smoothed input (where values are rounded to within $1/\epsilon$), first-price auctions yield $(1-O(\epsilon))$-approximate optimal revenue, a bound that applies universally to any market size and commodity quantity, as well as any side of the market. Furthermore, for the simpler case without quotas, we prove the stronger result that such auctions secure the exact maximal possible revenue from any $\epsilon$-smoothed profile. Conversely, for quota-heavy auctions, we construct an example showing that smooth data can result in a suboptimal revenue of $\Omega(\epsilon \log 1/\epsilon)$ relative to the best possible. Finally, we offer simple algorithms capable of boosting any suboptimal first-price auction revenue to near-optimality, either by repeating the auction multiple times or by applying it once but repeating the bidding process.

Addressing the challenge that achieving a Pareto efficient (PE) allocation is often computationally intractable, we concentrate on finding allocations that are both Pareto efficient and envy-free (EF). We establish that for two agents, an allocation satisfying both PE and EF exists if and only if it corresponds to the one derived from agents' most-preferred items within their respective valuation ranges, and we present a linear-time algorithm to compute it efficiently. For scenarios involving three or more agents, we introduce a new method, the Top Trading Cycle with Cycles (TCTC), to construct allocations meeting these criteria. Our approach integrates components of the Top Trading Cycle (TT) and Splitting (S) procedures, operating under the premise that each agent identifies their top-k preferred items within the EF framework. However, the significant computational resources required for both training and inference pose challenges for widespread deployment. To mitigate these issues, researchers frequently employ pruning techniques to reduce model complexity. A primary objective of pruning is reducing the number of weights, typically achieved by reducing weight precision. Yet, simply lowering precision does not guarantee effective compression, as it fails to reduce the overall model footprint. Consequently, a reduction in weight precision must be accompanied by a corresponding decrease in activation precision to ensure efficient compression. In this paper, we introduce a novel, differentiable end-to-end optimization method designed to discover optimal architectures for sparse, low-precision neural networks. Our approach simultaneously refines both structure and weights to maximize a user-defined metric while minimizing runtime latency resulting from mixed-precision execution on accelerators. Experiments demonstrate that our technique delivers state-of-the-art accuracy and inference speed across various benchmarks, including ImageNet classification and machine translation tasks.

Communication Computation Model (CCM) introduces a novel paradigm where objects interact by exchanging asynchronous, persistent messages. In this setup, one object solicits services from another by dispatching a message, which remains stored until the receiving object retrieves it to execute the necessary logic. Nevertheless, the inherent characteristics of CCA—specifically its asynchronicity and persistence—can introduce significant challenges regarding performance and programming complexity. previously been identified at distances exceeding those of our solar system; however, a newly discovered screen located in the Milky Way's own disk has recently come to light. This plasma concentration, termed DING (short for 'an anomalous source of radio scattering near the Galactic center'), forms a distinct scattering screen approximately 1.5 kiloparsecs from the Galactic center and exhibits a relatively low surface density of $10^4$ cm$^{-3}$. Characterizing screens as close to our Solar System as DING is vital for enhancing the precision of Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) measurements.

This article introduces a new, rapid algorithm for calculating such integrals, designed to complement the O$\rm B$N-N tree structure used in N-body simulations. This new method determines the gravitational potential generated by the halo's density profile, which extends to infinity and relies on either a generalized Spherically Symmetric N-body (SSNB) configuration or a Halos (HNB) setup. By deriving a series of analytically determined integrable forms, the algorithm enables the determination of the halo potential, which is subsequently utilized to calculate halo mass functions and their derivatives. The algorithm has been tested using the Millennium III simulation, demonstrating a performance improvement of approximately 100 times faster compared to standard $O(N)$ algorithms. This performance boost applies specifically to the calculation of the halo's own mass functions and functions, with the results' accuracy remaining within a $10^{-3}$ relative error margin when contrasted with exact analytical solutions.
